sections.html: Zungaro zungaro is one of the largest catfish species of South America. It reaches a length of up to 140 cm and a weight of up to 50 kg.

Such giants are only suitable for zoos, show aquariums and specialists with correspondingly large tanks. Juveniles of 15-20 cm length, still carrying the juvenile markings, have been imported from Brazil.
Not suited to the home aquarium due to its final adult size and its predatory instincts.
Z. zungaro occurs in the Amazon and Orinoco rivers. The very similar Z. jahu, which grows to exactly the same size, comes from the Paraná-Paraguay system.
South America: Amazon and Orinoco River basins. Introduced to fishing lakes in Thailand. Type locality: Tomependa, Río Marañon [Amazon River basin, Peru].

In the Amazon, this fish is found quite far upstream, in the main bed of the big tributaries with muddy bottom. Mainly piscivorous, it hunts at night, sometimes going into flood-prone areas of rivers. Some migrations in pursuit of migrating Triportheus and Anodus have been reported.

The adults are olive green with a white belly region, with villiform conical teeth in the palate and the pterygoid bone, forming developed patches. Juveniles and sub-adults are spotted and the adults are usually without spots. As this species grows the barbels shorten in length in relation to body size.
Sexually mature upon reaching 10 kg weight. The nursery ground is at the river mouths.

There were all kinds of debates about its name; for a long time it sailed under Pseudopimelodus zungaro or Paulicea luetkeni. Because of its gigantic size the species is difficult to study, and it undergoes an enormous colour change from a leopard-like patterned juvenile to a monochrome grey giant.

DNA studies suggest that there are other species besides the two generally recognized Zungaro species.

This large South American pim has been introduced to some fishing lakes in Thailand. Robust body with quadrangular and depressed head. Dorsal fin rays 1-6. Specimens measuring 130 cm and weighing 50 kg are not rare.

Etymology: The specific name zungaro comes from the native name "Zungaro", which is applied to many large pimelodids.

IUCN Red List: despite the little information available on this species, it has a wide range and no apparent threats. Therefore, it is assessed as Least Concern (IUCN 2023).
